meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The problem isn't that Johnny can't read. The problem isn't even that Johnny can't think. The problem is that Johnny doesn't know what thinking is; he confuses it with feeling'?
meta.ogDescription: Thomas Sowell wrote a version in Inside American Education (1993). The popular three-sentence wording is a later rewording, not his exact words.

answer.label: Not Sowell’s exact words — a paraphrase of his 1993 book
answer.authorDates: b. 30 June 1930 · American economist and social theorist
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Sowell’s. In Inside American Education (1993), ch. 1, p. 4, he wrote: “it is not merely that Johnny can’t read, or even that Johnny can’t think. Johnny doesn’t know what thinking is, because thinking is so often confused with feeling in many public schools.” The viral “The problem isn’t… he confuses it with feeling” version is a later rewording of that sentence.

source.excerpt: In short, it is not merely that Johnny can’t read, or even that Johnny can’t think. Johnny doesn’t know what thinking is, because thinking is so often confused with feeling in many public schools.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced entry lists the passage under Inside American Education (1993), “Ch. 1 : Decline, Deception, and Dogmas (p.4 Education),” and notes that it plays on Why Johnny Can’t Read. Wikiquote ↗

A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned copies returns the sentence “Johnny doesn’t know what thinking is, because thinking is so often confused with feeling in many public schools” in the 1993 Free Press edition of the book. Internet Archive full-text results ↗
When the book came out, Kirkus Reviews summed up its argument with the book’s own phrase, “Johnny doesn’t know what thinking is.” Kirkus Reviews ↗
The reworded version ending “he confuses it with feeling” turns up in the Archive’s full text only in later books by other writers, both crediting Sowell. Internet Archive full-text results ↗
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote notes the italics are in the original. The viral version swaps in “The problem isn’t… The problem isn’t even… The problem is…” and ends with “he confuses it with feeling,” a phrase the book does not use.

author.bio: Thomas Sowell (born June 30, 1930, in Gastonia, North Carolina) is an American economist and social theorist and a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution. He wrote dozens of books on economics, race, culture and education, including Inside American Education (1993). He also wrote a nationally syndicated column, which he ended in December 2016.

misattribution.heading: Right author, reworded quote
misattribution.intro: This is not a quote pinned on Sowell out of nowhere. He did make the point, in a 1993 book. What travels online is a smoother, punchier rewording that he never wrote.

items.why: The book reads “it is not merely that Johnny can’t read, or even that Johnny can’t think. Johnny doesn’t know what thinking is, because thinking is so often confused with feeling in many public schools” (Wikiquote ↗). The repeated “The problem isn’t…” structure and the closing “he confuses it with feeling” are not in the book. The Archive’s full text finds that phrasing only in later books by other writers (search results ↗).

Goodreads’ widely liked entry gives the reworded version under Sowell’s name with no book or source, and notes that community-submitted quotes are not verified (Goodreads ↗). By contrast, a 2022 post imported from Sowell’s own site feed uses the book’s wording (Thomas Sowell’s blog feed ↗).
Sowell’s opening plays on the title of Rudolf Flesch’s 1955 book Why Johnny Can’t Read (Wikipedia ↗). The title is Flesch’s, but the “doesn’t know what thinking is” point is Sowell’s.

misattribution.truthLine: Sowell made this point in Inside American Education (1993), ch. 1, p. 4: “Johnny doesn’t know what thinking is, because thinking is so often confused with feeling in many public schools.” The popular “The problem isn’t that Johnny can’t read” text is a paraphrase of it (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Inside American Education (The Free Press, 1993) was Sowell’s critique of American schooling, from primary and secondary schools through colleges and universities (Wikipedia ↗). The “Johnny” sentence sums up the opening chapter’s case, and early reviewers picked it out. Kirkus used it to sum up the book (Kirkus Reviews ↗).

Over time, quote collections reshaped the sentence into a three-step “The problem isn’t…” build-up with a sharper ending. That version is easier to share, but it is not what Sowell printed. His version also places the confusion “in many public schools.”
